submission.natural_language_explanation: N1361+ fires when the model is reading text that is not plain narrative English - LaTeX/mathematical notation, markup, or text with corrupted non-ASCII bytes - and the peak lands on the token that carries the structure rather than the content of that text: a LaTeX group/environment command right after a backslash ('left', 'right', 'begin', 'end' at 1.8-3.7 after ' \', versus 0.0-0.7 for the same strings as ordinary English words), a math delimiter ('$.', '$,'), a citation bracket (' ['), a line break, a raw byte fragment of a multi-byte character (the scan's 1,129 active non-ASCII tokens are 30% of the active set), a piece of a multi-token name or technical term ('ou' in Chou, 'mann' in Gutmann, ' bes' in besieging, ' d' in drench), and in technical prose the clause's finite auxiliary, copula, modal or pronoun subject ('We', 'we', 'You', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'be', 'will', 'can', 'then', 'now', 'first'). It is at zero on plain narrative English, on determiners, prepositions and conjunctions even inside technical sentences ('the' 0.002, 'of' 0.003, 'a' 0.010, 'that' 0.007, 'Our' 0.00), and on the same sentences with their technical vocabulary replaced by everyday words ('We' after a physics sentence 1.74, after 'The cat is not sleeping in the warm room' 0.32).

rival_explanations: Narrower: the pole is only a broken-token / subword-fragment detector (a sibling of L5/N142+ and L5/N1477+), and its firings on correctly tokenized technical English ('We', 'is', 'are', 'then') are the same fragment feature seen through rare tokens; on clean, correctly tokenized technical prose with no split words it should stay near zero, so the register counterfactuals above should fail.

Broader: it is a technical/academic-register detector that lifts activation across dense mathematical prose whatever the token, so determiners and prepositions inside a math paper ('the', 'of', 'in') should fire too and plain narrative should be uniformly at zero; the apparent token selectivity would be an artefact of which tokens happen to sit at the sampled positions.

Boundary reading: it detects the seams of text segments (sentence-final periods, newlines, colons, opening delimiters) rather than any non-prose content, so it should fire equally on the same boundary in plain narrative, and the LaTeX/broken-byte peaks are just boundary positions that happen to carry rare tokens.

Here are some specific measures you can take to resolve other sources of disconnections:
1. Check your phone line for obvious signs of noise. You can do this by picking-up your telephone (while you are not connected) and dialing a digit to eliminate the tone. Listen carefully to the dead air for any static, crackles, voices, etc. If you hear any of this, chances are your modem will not keep a firm connection. If your modem uses a dedicated phone line, you may have a noise problem and not realize it. Connect a telephone to the line so you can listen for noise.
Realize that the noise you hear could be caused by a worn cord, a poorly-wired wall jack, the phone itself, or some other problem in your house. If possible, also check for noise from another location in the house, or using a different telephone.
You can completely eliminate your house wiring as the source of the problem if have access to your Network Interface Device (NID). This is a box mounted on the side of your house, usually near the electric meter, where your phone company's line connects to your house wiring. If you can get a long enough phone cord or move the computer to a room near the NID, you can open the box and disconnect the modular phone plug inside (your house wiring) from its jack (your phone company's line). (Be sure to read any instructions or warnings on the box.) Now connect your modem line directly to the jack, thereby bypassing your house wiring. Connect the Internet, and if the disconnections continue, your inside wiring is not the problem.
You will need to contact your local phone company about any possible noise problems. adversarial_test_results.prompt:
## 3. Renormalization of the two-point function

We work in Euclidean signature and regulate the momentum integrals with a hard cutoff $\Lambda$. The bare propagator takes the form
\[
G_0(p) = \frac{1}{p^2 + m^2}
\]
and the one-loop correction is obtained by contracting the vertices in the usual way. After a Wick rotation the integrand falls off like $1/p^4$, so the superficial degree of divergence is finite for $d < 4$ and the counterterm is a mass renormalization. We then absorb the divergent piece into the definition of $m^2$ and verify that the residue at the pole is unchanged. A short calculation gives
\[
\delta m^2 = \frac{g^2}{16\pi^2} \Lambda^2 + O(g^4),
\]
which agrees with the result quoted in the appendix. The remaining finite part is scheme dependent and is fixed by the condition that the propagator has unit residue at $p^2 = -m^2$. It is worth emphasizing that no wave-function renormalization is needed at this order, and that the same conclusion holds for the fermionic sector once the vertex correction is included. We therefore keep the tree-level normalization throughout and refer to the appendix for the algebraic details.

readings.explanation: N1361+ fires when the model is reading text that is not plain narrative English - LaTeX/mathematical notation, markup, or text with corrupted non-ASCII bytes - and the peak lands on the token that carries the structure rather than the content of that text: a LaTeX group/environment command right after a backslash ('left', 'right', 'begin', 'end' at 1.8-3.7 after ' \', versus 0.0-0.7 for the same strings as ordinary English words), a math delimiter ('$.', '$,'), a citation bracket (' ['), a line break, a raw byte fragment of a multi-byte character (the scan's 1,129 active non-ASCII tokens are 30% of the active set), a piece of a multi-token name or technical term ('ou' in Chou, 'mann' in Gutmann, ' bes' in besieging, ' d' in drench), and in technical prose the clause's finite auxiliary, copula, modal or pronoun subject ('We', 'we', 'You', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'be', 'will', 'can', 'then', 'now', 'first'). It is at zero on plain narrative English, on determiners, prepositions and conjunctions even inside technical sentences ('the' 0.002, 'of' 0.003, 'a' 0.010, 'that' 0.007, 'Our' 0.00), and on the same sentences with their technical vocabulary replaced by everyday words ('We' after a physics sentence 1.74, after 'The cat is not sleeping in the warm room' 0.32).

Narrower: the pole is only a broken-token / subword-fragment detector (a sibling of L5/N142+ and L5/N1477+), and its firings on correctly tokenized technical English ('We', 'is', 'are', 'then') are the same fragment feature seen through rare tokens; on clean, correctly tokenized technical prose with no split words it should stay near zero, so the register counterfactuals above should fail.

Broader: it is a technical/academic-register detector that lifts activation across dense mathematical prose whatever the token, so determiners and prepositions inside a math paper ('the', 'of', 'in') should fire too and plain narrative should be uniformly at zero; the apparent token selectivity would be an artefact of which tokens happen to sit at the sampled positions.

Boundary reading: it detects the seams of text segments (sentence-final periods, newlines, colons, opening delimiters) rather than any non-prose content, so it should fire equally on the same boundary in plain narrative, and the LaTeX/broken-byte peaks are just boundary positions that happen to carry rare tokens.
